title: The Smallest Lantern
moral: Never think your small good deed is useless. A little kindness in the right place can help many people.

pages.text:
The apartment children were preparing for the evening light display.

Everyone had to bring one lantern and hang it near the garden path. By sunset, the whole path would glow.

Rida had made a small lantern from an old jam jar. She painted yellow dots on it and tied a blue ribbon around the top.

It was simple, but she liked it.

Then she saw Vihaan's lantern.

It was tall, colourful, and shaped like a palace.

"Mine has three windows," Vihaan said proudly.

Rida looked at her jar.

It had no windows. It had once held mango pickle.

Her little brother Sameer picked it up and sniffed it.

"It still smells like achaar," he said.

Rida snatched it back. "It does not!"

Sameer smiled. "A little."

At sunset, the children began hanging their lanterns. Big lanterns. Star lanterns. Flower lanterns.

Rida slowly placed hers at the end of the path, behind a bush. Nobody would notice it there.

Just then, the lights near the gate went off.

"Oh no," said Uncle Raj. "The wire is loose."

The first part of the path became dark. The younger children stood near the gate, unsure where to walk.

Rida looked at her small lantern.

It had a candle inside.

She picked it up and placed it near the dark step.

The little flame glowed through the yellow dots.

"Now I can see!" said a small boy.

Another child followed. Then another.

Soon, everyone was walking safely past the gate.

Vihaan came and stood beside her.

"Your lantern helped the most," he said.

Rida looked surprised. "But it is the smallest."

Uncle Raj smiled. "Small lights are still lights."

Sameer leaned close and whispered, "And this one smells brave."

Rida laughed.

Later, when all the lights were fixed, the garden looked beautiful. But many people stopped near Rida's small jar lantern.

It did not look like a palace.

It did not have windows.

But it had stood where the darkness was.

Rida looked at its tiny flame and felt something warm inside her.

Sometimes the smallest light can make the biggest difference.
